cards.title: Conscientious Objection Tests Whether States Can Compel Citizens to Fight
cards.background: The piece was published on 15 May 2026, International Conscientious Objectors’ Day, and focuses on people who refuse military service or combat participation on moral, religious, or political grounds. It asks what happens to conscientious objectors today and what consequences they face when they refuse to fight in wars. The article is framed around the contemporary treatment of objectors rather than a single country case, so the relevant debate terrain is the balance between state security needs and individual rights.

prop_args.thesis: Protecting conscientious objectors strengthens liberal legitimacy and prevents states from turning war-making into an unchecked coercive project.
mechanisms: First, it preserves the basic liberal principle that the state cannot force citizens to directly participate in killing against their deepest moral convictions. This is because (1) conscription is the most extreme form of state coercion, (2) forcing combat service creates irreversible psychological and moral harm, and (3) allowing exemptions signals that citizenship does not mean total surrender of conscience.

Second, it improves the quality of military and political decision-making by raising the cost of war. Three reasons: one, if governments know they cannot automatically absorb every eligible body, they are less able to treat war as a low-cost policy tool; two, visible objection creates public scrutiny and can expose unjust or unnecessary conflicts; three, it reduces the risk of sending unwilling soldiers into combat, which can undermine unit cohesion and operational effectiveness.

Third, it reduces long-term social backlash against the state and the military. This matters because (1) punishing objectors harshly can radicalize anti-war sentiment and deepen distrust in institutions, (2) accommodating dissent makes wartime mobilization more politically sustainable, and (3) societies that respect conscience are better able to reconcile after conflict rather than inherit a generation of traumatized, alienated veterans and refusers.

opp_args.thesis: In wartime, states must be able to compel service because broad exemption regimes undermine deterrence, fairness, and survival.
mechanisms: First, widespread conscientious objection can hollow out military manpower and create unequal burden-sharing. One, if enough people opt out, the state cannot field sufficient forces in emergencies; two, exemptions often shift the costs of defense onto poorer or less politically connected citizens who cannot avoid service; three, selective refusal can create a free-rider problem where people enjoy security without contributing to it.

Second, allowing refusal on subjective grounds invites abuse and weakens the rule of law. One, governments cannot reliably verify whether every claim is sincere, so the system becomes vulnerable to opportunistic evasion; two, broad exemptions create administrative inconsistency and resentment among those who comply; three, in existential wars the state needs clear, uniform obligations rather than case-by-case moral arbitration.

Third, the state’s duty to protect the population can outweigh individual conscience in extreme circumstances. This matters because (1) if a country loses a war, civilians may face occupation, repression, or mass death, (2) the moral cost of one person’s refusal can be borne by many others if defense fails, and (3) democratic societies can still protect conscience through non-combat roles, alternative service, or postwar amnesties without fully exempting people from national duty.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the harm of coercing individuals is greater than the harm of weakening collective defense. Prop wins if the round is about rights, legitimacy, and the precedent of state violence; opp wins if the round is about existential security and the need for enforceable obligations under wartime pressure.

cards.title: US-Mediated Israel-Lebanon Talks Expose Whether Ceasefires Can Hold Without Enforcement
cards.background: On 15 May 2026, the first of two days of US-mediated ambassador-level talks between Israel and Lebanon concluded in Washington. The talks came days before a ceasefire between the two sides was due to expire on Sunday. According to the report, Israel had killed 512 Lebanese since the ceasefire took effect on 17 April 2026.

prop_args.thesis: US-mediated talks are necessary to prevent a ceasefire collapse and create even a minimal diplomatic channel for de-escalation.
mechanisms: First, the talks create a direct crisis-management channel between two states that otherwise lack trust and regular communication. This matters because (1) it reduces the chance of miscalculation during a fragile ceasefire, (2) it lets the US translate red lines into concrete commitments, and (3) it gives both sides a face-saving way to extend restraint without appearing weak domestically.

Second, US mediation is the only actor with enough leverage to keep both sides at the table. Three reasons: one, Washington can condition military assistance and diplomatic cover on compliance; two, it can coordinate with allies to raise the cost of escalation; three, it can offer sequencing and verification mechanisms that neither side would accept from the other directly.

Third, even a limited extension of the ceasefire has major humanitarian value because it prevents further civilian deaths and buys time for broader negotiations. This matters because the ceasefire has already been violated enough to kill 512 Lebanese since 17 April, so every additional day of restraint directly lowers the immediate death toll and reduces the risk of a wider regional war.

opp_args.thesis: The talks are mostly performative because without enforcement capacity, ceasefires between asymmetric enemies collapse once battlefield incentives return.
mechanisms: First, the talks do not solve the core commitment problem. One, both sides have strong incentives to use the ceasefire to regroup, rearm, or improve bargaining positions; two, there is no neutral enforcement body on the ground with the ability to punish violations in real time; three, if one side believes the other is cheating, it will defect pre-emptively rather than wait to be exploited.

Second, US mediation can actually entrench impunity if it substitutes diplomacy for accountability. One, Israel faces limited immediate costs for continued strikes if Washington keeps hosting talks; two, Lebanon can be pressured into concessions without reciprocal guarantees; three, the process may normalize a pattern where ceasefires become temporary pauses rather than durable settlements.

Third, the talks may buy time for escalation rather than peace. One, a short extension can allow both sides to reposition militarily; two, the expiration deadline creates a cliff-edge that increases incentives for last-minute brinkmanship; three, if the ceasefire expires without a broader political settlement, the conflict resumes with even less trust than before.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether diplomacy can change incentives faster than violence can reset them. Prop wins if you prioritize immediate civilian protection and the value of a credible de-escalation channel; opp wins if you think the absence of enforcement means the talks merely manage optics while the underlying security dilemma remains untouched.

THBT external powers should prioritize ceasefire maintenance over final-status negotiations in active conflicts
THP a world where fragile ceasefires are backed by major-power mediation

cards.title: US-China Farm Trade Truce Could Reopen Soy and Corn Markets, But At the Cost of Strategic Leverage
cards.background: Soybean futures edged higher after US President Donald Trump said he was optimistic about striking a deal with China, raising expectations that China may resume purchases of US agricultural exports. The article centers on soybeans and corn, two major US farm exports that are highly exposed to Chinese demand. China is the world's largest buyer of soybeans, so even signals of renewed buying can move global commodity prices quickly.

prop_args.thesis: A US-China agricultural deal is economically rational because it restores market access for American farmers and reduces volatility in a strategically important export sector.
mechanisms: First, it directly restores demand for US crops. This is because (1) China is the world's largest soybean buyer, so even partial reopening of purchases can absorb large US surpluses, (2) higher export demand lifts farmgate prices and futures, and (3) that price support immediately improves cash flow for farmers and agribusinesses across the Midwest.

Second, it reduces uncertainty in a sector that is highly exposed to trade shocks. Three reasons: one, farmers make planting and storage decisions months in advance and need predictable export channels; two, volatile tariff wars force costly hedging and inventory misallocation; three, a deal lowers the risk premium on US agricultural commodities, which stabilizes credit conditions for rural lenders and input suppliers.

Third, it creates a broader bargaining channel that can spill into wider economic de-escalation. This matters because agricultural trade is politically salient in both countries, so a limited deal can build trust, demonstrate that negotiated concessions are possible, and create a template for future agreements on industrial goods or tariffs.

opp_args.thesis: Any short-term gain from selling more crops to China is outweighed by the strategic and structural costs of making US agriculture dependent on Chinese political goodwill.
mechanisms: First, it increases leverage for China over a politically sensitive US constituency. one, if Chinese purchases become the difference between profit and loss, Beijing can threaten to cut demand to extract concessions; two, that weakens US negotiating power in future disputes; three, it turns farm exports into a hostage asset rather than a stable market.

Second, it entrenches a fragile trade pattern instead of fixing underlying competitiveness problems. one, farmers become reliant on a single giant buyer rather than diversified markets; two, that concentration exposes them to sudden policy reversals, sanctions, or retaliation; three, it discourages long-term adjustment into value-added processing or alternative export destinations.

Third, it normalizes a cycle of tariff escalation and partial rollback that creates chronic instability. one, markets price in temporary truces rather than durable rules; two, firms underinvest because they expect future disruptions; three, the result is repeated boom-bust pricing that hurts both producers and consumers more than a stable decoupling would.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between immediate farm income and long-term strategic dependence. Prop wins if the round is about near-term economic welfare for US producers; opp wins if the motion is about bargaining power or resilience, because China’s ability to switch purchases on and off creates a structural leverage asymmetry.

cards.title: China’s Promised Farm Purchases Become a Bargaining Chip in the US Trade War
cards.background: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the Trump administration expects China to make "dramatic" agricultural purchases from the United States. The comment comes amid an ongoing tariff confrontation between Washington and Beijing, with the administration also preparing a tiered tariff system for steel and aluminum imports to simplify a process that has frustrated American companies for months. The article frames farm purchases as part of broader trade negotiations rather than a standalone agricultural deal.

prop_args.thesis: Using agricultural purchases as leverage is a rational way to convert trade conflict into a visible win for domestic producers while keeping pressure on China to negotiate on broader terms.
mechanisms: First, it creates a direct political payoff for the administration and farm states. This is because (1) soybeans, corn, pork, and other commodities are highly visible to rural constituencies, (2) even a partial rebound in Chinese demand can stabilize prices and farm incomes, and (3) the White House can present purchases as proof that tariffs are extracting concessions rather than just imposing costs.

Second, it can function as a bargaining chip that de-escalates the wider trade war without requiring immediate structural concessions. Three reasons: one, China can buy agricultural goods relatively quickly compared with reconfiguring industrial supply chains; two, the US can claim success while leaving room for follow-on talks on industrial tariffs and market access; three, both sides can frame the deal as reciprocal, which lowers the domestic political cost of compromise.

Third, it helps preserve US leverage over China’s broader economic behavior. This matters because if China wants tariff relief or predictability, it has to demonstrate compliance through measurable purchases, which gives the US a monitoring mechanism and a way to punish non-performance in future rounds.

opp_args.thesis: Treating farm purchases as a trade victory is mostly cosmetic and risks locking the US into a cycle where China buys politically useful goods without changing the underlying imbalance.
mechanisms: First, the purchases are easy for China to manipulate and therefore weak as a durable concession. One, Beijing can front-load purchases to create headlines and then reduce them later; two, it can redirect state-owned or state-influenced buying to meet quotas without changing market access; three, it can use agricultural imports as a low-cost pressure valve while keeping barriers on higher-value US exports and technology.

Second, this strategy entrenches uncertainty for American businesses rather than solving it. One, firms cannot plan around ad hoc tariff bargaining and seasonal purchase promises; two, the tiered tariff system suggests continuing administrative discretion, which increases compliance costs and lobbying; three, repeated trade brinkmanship encourages firms to diversify away from the US-China corridor, reducing the long-run benefit of any one-off purchase surge.

Third, it can worsen the strategic relationship by making agriculture hostage to geopolitical escalation. One, China can retaliate by cutting farm purchases whenever tensions rise; two, US farmers become dependent on politically engineered demand rather than open-market access; three, this makes the sector more vulnerable to future shocks and reduces the credibility of trade rules.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the purchases are a real concession or just a reversible headline. Prop wins if the round is about immediate domestic relief and signaling leverage; opp wins if the round is about long-run trade stability, because ad hoc buying does little to change the structural dependence on Chinese political decisions.

cards.title: Japan’s Fiscal Restraint Collides With Rising Bond Yields and Oil-Shock Growth Risks
cards.background: Japan’s finance minister Satsuki Katayama said there is “no need” for an extra budget even as Japanese government bond yields rise. The statement came during the IMF and World Bank Spring Meetings in Washington, DC on April 16, 2026. At the same meetings, the IMF downgraded its global growth outlook after a war in the Middle East triggered a major oil shock, warning that growth could deteriorate further if the conflict drags on and energy infrastructure is badly damaged.

prop_args.thesis: Japan should avoid an extra budget because fiscal discipline now prevents a debt-market spiral and preserves room for targeted support later.
mechanisms: First, refusing an extra budget anchors expectations that the government will not monetize every shock with fresh borrowing. This is because (1) Japan already has one of the highest public debt burdens in the world, so markets are highly sensitive to any signal of fiscal slippage; (2) higher bond yields mean debt-service costs rise mechanically, so new spending today compounds future interest burdens; (3) credible restraint can reduce the risk premium on Japanese government bonds by signaling that policymakers will not turn a temporary oil shock into a permanent fiscal expansion.

Second, keeping powder dry improves the quality of future crisis response. Three reasons: one, if the Middle East shock worsens or energy infrastructure is hit, Japan can still deploy a larger, more targeted package later; two, a delayed response allows the government to better identify which sectors actually need support rather than spraying cash across the economy; three, avoiding an early blanket budget reduces the chance of politically sticky spending that becomes hard to unwind.

Third, fiscal restraint protects the yen and broader macro stability. This matters because a larger deficit-financed package can weaken confidence in Japan’s fiscal trajectory, push yields higher, and crowd out private investment; by contrast, restraint supports market confidence, limits imported inflation from a weaker currency, and reduces the probability that the oil shock becomes a broader inflation-and-rate spiral.

opp_args.thesis: Japan should pass an extra budget because the oil shock and rising yields make immediate fiscal support necessary to prevent a deeper slowdown.
mechanisms: First, the shock is external and immediate, so waiting for normal budget cycles is too slow. One, higher energy prices hit households and firms right away through electricity, transport, and input costs; two, if the IMF is already downgrading growth, the economy is likely operating below potential and needs demand support; three, a timely supplementary budget can cushion the shock before layoffs, bankruptcies, and consumption cuts become entrenched.

Second, targeted fiscal support can actually stabilize markets rather than scare them. One, if the government uses the budget to subsidize energy costs or support vulnerable sectors, it reduces the probability of a hard landing and therefore lowers default risk across the economy; two, a credible package can be paired with medium-term consolidation to reassure bondholders; three, if yields are rising because growth is weakening, austerity can be self-defeating by worsening the debt-to-GDP ratio through lower nominal growth.

Third, the political economy of Japan makes inaction costly. One, households facing imported inflation are more likely to lose confidence in the government if it appears passive; two, firms need certainty on energy and operating costs to keep hiring and investing; three, a supplementary budget can buy time and social stability while the external shock plays out, preventing a temporary crisis from becoming a structural recession.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether rising yields are a warning to tighten or a symptom of a growth shock that requires stabilization. Prop wins if the round prioritizes long-run fiscal credibility and market signaling; opp wins if it proves the oil shock is immediate, broad-based, and likely to make restraint pro-cyclical.

THBT governments should prioritize fiscal restraint over stimulus when bond yields rise

cards.title: US-Cuba Backchannel Talks Expose the Limits of Sanctions-First Coercion
cards.background: Cuba said CIA director John Ratcliffe met Cuban officials in Havana on Thursday to improve dialogue between the two countries. The meeting came one day after protests in Havana over a fuel crisis, with Cuba’s energy minister saying the country had completely run out of diesel and fuel oil and that the national grid was in a "critical" state. Washington imposed a fuel blockade in January, while President Donald Trump has also added sanctions and floated taking over the island; meanwhile, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has offered $100m in aid if it is distributed through the Catholic Church rather than the Cuban government.

prop_args.thesis: Backchannel engagement is the only realistic way to prevent sanctions from turning Cuba into a permanent humanitarian and geopolitical flashpoint.
mechanisms: First, direct talks create a de-escalation channel that sanctions alone cannot provide. This is because (1) Cuba is already in a severe energy emergency with "absolutely no fuel oil" and "absolutely no diesel," (2) the state is facing street protests and 22-hour blackouts, so pressure is already producing instability rather than policy change, and (3) a covert or diplomatic channel lets both sides test concessions without forcing public capitulation.

Second, engagement improves US leverage by separating humanitarian relief from regime survival narratives. Three reasons: one, Cuba can more credibly accept aid if it is framed as practical relief rather than ideological surrender; two, the US can condition limited easing on verifiable steps like non-hostility and migration cooperation; three, bypassing the government entirely risks making aid look like an opposition-building tool, which hardens Cuban resistance.

Third, dialogue reduces the risk of escalation into a broader security confrontation. This matters because (1) Cuba is explicitly trying to prove it is not a threat to US national security, (2) the US has already escalated with sanctions and terrorism-list allegations, and (3) once both sides lock into maximalist rhetoric, even routine humanitarian or intelligence issues become securitized and harder to unwind.

opp_args.thesis: Talking to Havana legitimizes an authoritarian regime while weakening the only pressure that can force meaningful change.
mechanisms: First, engagement gives the Cuban government diplomatic breathing room without requiring reforms. One, the regime can point to talks with a CIA director as proof of international legitimacy; two, it can use negotiations to split US hawks from moderates; three, it can keep domestic repression intact while blaming shortages on the blockade.

Second, sanctions and isolation remain the strongest coercive tool because the regime is structurally vulnerable to economic pressure. One, Cuba has no fuel reserves and a collapsing grid, so external pressure bites hard; two, the government has historically prioritized regime survival over liberalization, meaning concessions are unlikely unless costs become unbearable; three, aid routed through the state risks being captured by the same apparatus that created the crisis.

Third, bypassing Havana through church-led aid is more effective than normalizing the state. One, it delivers humanitarian relief directly to civilians without strengthening the security services; two, it preserves leverage by making assistance conditional; three, it avoids the moral hazard of rewarding a government that has repeatedly used anti-US rhetoric to deflect blame for domestic failure.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether pressure or dialogue better changes Cuban state behavior under acute economic collapse. Pro side wins if the judge prioritizes immediate humanitarian stabilization and de-escalation; opposition wins if the judge thinks legitimacy and leverage are lost the moment Washington starts treating the regime as a normal negotiating partner.

cards.title: Australia’s Housing Crisis Becomes a Climate Inequality Trap Under High-Emissions Pathways
cards.background: University of Sydney researchers modelled Australia’s housing market using two decades of public data and tested it against IPCC-style social and economic pathways. They found climate change worsens housing affordability under both low- and high-emissions futures, but the effects are much worse in a fossil-fuelled future, with homelessness projected to be four times higher by 2036. Australia has committed under the Paris Agreement to cut emissions 43% below 2005 levels by 2030, 62-70% by 2035, and reach net zero by 2050.

prop_args.thesis: Climate policy must be integrated into housing policy because high-emissions futures directly worsen affordability and massively expand homelessness.
mechanisms: First, climate change raises the cost of housing through multiple channels at once. This is because (1) insurance premiums rise as flood, fire, and storm risk increases, (2) repair and maintenance costs increase as homes face more extreme weather damage, and (3) lenders and buyers price in higher long-run risk, which pushes down supply and raises rents relative to incomes.

Second, the burden is highly regressive, so the same shock hits renters and low-income households far harder than owners. Three reasons: one, renters have less ability to absorb rent increases through wealth or refinancing; two, low-income households are more exposed to insecure housing and eviction; three, people already experiencing homelessness are pushed further out of the market, which is why the study finds homelessness could be four times higher by 2036 under a high-emissions future.

Third, this is not a marginal environmental externality but a structural inequality amplifier. This matters because housing is the main asset and cost base for most households, so when climate risk is ignored in policy design, every new housing intervention can accidentally deepen inequality unless it is stress-tested against climate scenarios.

opp_args.thesis: Housing affordability is driven primarily by domestic policy failures and macroeconomic conditions, so climate change is a secondary factor that should not dominate housing reform.
mechanisms: First, the immediate drivers of affordability are still conventional market variables. One, mortgage rates and credit conditions affect monthly repayments far more directly than long-run climate projections; two, land supply, zoning, and planning restrictions constrain new housing supply; three, wage growth and income distribution determine whether households can absorb rent increases.

Second, climate-focused housing policy risks misallocating scarce political and fiscal attention. One, governments may spend on resilience measures while failing to fix the core supply shortage; two, broad climate rules can raise construction costs and slow delivery; three, the people most in need of housing need immediate supply and income support, not only long-term scenario planning.

Third, the worst climate impacts are uncertain and unevenly distributed, so policy should prioritize proven interventions. One, the study is model-based and depends on assumptions about emissions pathways and adaptation; two, households can partially adapt through insurance, relocation, and building standards; three, governments should not overstate climate as the main cause of homelessness when structural housing shortages already explain much of the crisis.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether climate change is a background risk or a direct driver of housing inequality. Prop wins if the round is about future-proofing policy and protecting the most vulnerable, because the harms compound over time and are hardest to reverse once homelessness rises; Opp wins if the judge prioritizes immediate affordability, since supply, rates, and zoning are the more proximate levers.

cards.title: Trump-Xi Summit Tests Whether Trade Concessions Can Buy Strategic Restraint on Taiwan and Iran
cards.background: Bloomberg's 'Balance of Power: Late Edition' covered President Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and the question of whether the summit produced meaningful outcomes on trade, Taiwan, and Iran. Representative Marlin Stutzman (R-IN) said China reopening to US beef is a 'big deal' for farmers and called Trump’s Beijing trip 'one of the most consequential' of his presidency. Representative Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) argued Xi is projecting confidence and said the US should 'watch what he does' after Trump said Xi would not send weapons to Iran.

prop_args.thesis: The summit is valuable because limited trade openings can be leveraged into broader strategic de-escalation with China.
mechanisms: First, trade concessions create a bargaining channel that makes future crisis management easier. This is because (1) both sides now have something tangible to defend, (2) repeated economic engagement increases the cost of immediate retaliation, and (3) leaders can package cooperation on beef, market access, or tariffs as proof that dialogue works.

Second, even modest commercial wins can reduce pressure for escalation in the bilateral relationship. Three reasons: one, US exporters and farm states gain a constituency for stability; two, Beijing can signal restraint without appearing weak; three, the summit establishes a precedent that the relationship is managed through deal-making rather than confrontation.

Third, if Trump can extract even partial commitments on Taiwan or Iran-related behavior, that improves deterrence through ambiguity and direct leader-to-leader signaling. This matters because public commitments from Xi, even if imperfect, raise the political cost of later violations and give Washington a clearer basis for coalition-building and sanctions.

opp_args.thesis: The summit is dangerous because economic concessions are unlikely to change China's core strategic behavior and may instead reward coercion.
mechanisms: First, China can pocket trade gains while preserving its leverage on Taiwan and Iran. One, Beijing can reopen select markets like beef without altering military or diplomatic pressure on Taiwan; two, it can make verbal assurances that are cheap to give and hard to verify; three, it can continue supporting partners or proxies indirectly while denying direct weapons transfers.

Second, deal-making may weaken US deterrence by signaling that Washington prioritizes short-term commercial wins over security red lines. One, allies may read concessions as evidence the US will trade away strategic concerns for domestic political optics; two, China may infer that coercive pressure works because it produces negotiations; three, this encourages future brinkmanship around Taiwan, sanctions, and export controls.

Third, the summit can create false confidence and reduce vigilance. One, leaders may overinterpret a successful meeting as evidence of durable moderation; two, enforcement problems mean promises on Iran or Taiwan can be reversed after the spotlight fades; three, the real test is post-summit behavior, not summit rhetoric.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether economic engagement changes China's incentives or merely buys time while Beijing preserves strategic options. The opposition has the structural advantage if the round centers on verification and enforcement, because trade wins are immediate and visible while restraint on Taiwan or Iran is ambiguous and easy to evade.

THBT the US should pursue summit diplomacy with China despite unresolved Taiwan and Iran tensions
THP a world where major powers use economic access as leverage for strategic non-proliferation commitments

cards.title: US-Iran War Turns the Strait of Hormuz Into a Test of Great-Power Alignment
cards.region: Iran / United States / China / BRICS / Gulf
cards.background: On 15 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported live updates on the Iran war as US President Donald Trump’s visit to China was overshadowed by the conflict with Tehran. The White House said Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discussed keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, with Xi agreeing that the waterway "must remain open to support the free flow of energy." Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iranians would "never bow to pressure" and urged BRICS states to condemn the US-Israel war on Iran as a violation of international law.

prop_args.thesis: The war strengthens US leverage over China and the BRICS by forcing them to choose between rhetorical anti-Western solidarity and the material need for stable energy flows.
mechanisms: First, the Strait of Hormuz becomes a coercive chokepoint. This is because (1) China is structurally dependent on Gulf energy imports, (2) any threat to shipping immediately raises insurance, freight, and refinery costs, and (3) the US can frame itself as the guarantor of maritime order while Iran is cast as the disruptor.

Second, Iran’s appeal to BRICS exposes the bloc’s internal contradictions. Three reasons: one, BRICS members have divergent threat perceptions and trade interests, two, most members do not want to be dragged into a direct confrontation with Washington over Tehran, and three, public condemnation is cheap but meaningful material support is costly.

Third, the crisis gives the US a diplomatic wedge against China. This matters because Washington can use energy security as a bargaining chip, pressure Beijing to restrain Tehran, and split any emerging anti-US alignment by making China responsible for keeping global markets stable.

opp_args.thesis: The war accelerates anti-US alignment by convincing China and BRICS that Washington is willing to weaponize force and energy insecurity to discipline rivals.
mechanisms: First, the conflict reinforces the narrative of US unilateralism. One, Iran can present itself as a victim of US-Israel aggression, two, BRICS states can treat the war as evidence that international law is selectively enforced, and three, this makes anti-Western coordination politically easier even if it is not immediately military.

Second, the Strait of Hormuz crisis increases the incentive to diversify away from US-controlled systems. One, China and other importers will seek alternative supply routes and reserve arrangements, two, they will deepen energy and payment cooperation with sanctioned states, and three, this reduces long-run US leverage even if the immediate crisis is contained.

Third, the war can backfire by hardening Iranian resistance. One, Araghchi’s statement that Iranians will "never bow to pressure" signals elite resolve, two, external attack often consolidates domestic support around the regime, and three, a more defiant Iran is more likely to coordinate with revisionist partners rather than capitulate.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the crisis creates dependence on US-led stability or resentment against US coercion. Prop has the structural advantage in the short term because energy markets and shipping routes force immediate pragmatism, but Opp can win if they prove the war produces durable anti-US bloc formation rather than just temporary crisis management.

THBT BRICS should condemn the US-Israel war on Iran
TH, as China, would publicly side with Iran in the current conflict
THP a world where great powers are forced to choose between energy security and ideological alignment in the Middle East
